entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 2Ti 4:1-22 . entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18230"/><div sID="gen37792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18230"/><hi type="bold">2. Preach--</hi>literally, "proclaim as a herald." The term for the discourses in the synagogue was daraschoth; the corresponding Greek term (implying dialectial style, dialogue, and discussion, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.4">18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19">19</reference>) is applied in Acts to discourses in the Christian Church. Justin Martyr [Apology, 2], describes the order of public worship, "On Sunday all meet and the writings of the apostles and prophets are read; then the president delivers a discourse; after this all stand up and pray; then there is offered bread and wine and water; the president likewise prays and gives thanks, and the people solemnly assent, saying, Amen." The bishops and presbyters had the right and duty to preach, but they sometimes called on deacons, and even laymen, to preach. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 6.19]; in this the Church imitated the synagogue (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.17-Luke.4.22">Lu 4:17-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.15">Ac 13:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen37792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be instant--</hi>that is, urgent, earnest, in the whole work of the ministry.<div eID="gen37793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in season, out of season--</hi>that is, at all seasons; whether they regard your speaking as seasonable or unseasonable. "Just as the fountains, though none may draw from them, still flow on; and the rivers, though none drink of them, still run; so must we do all on our part in speaking, though none give heed to us" [Chrysostom, Homily, 30, vol. 5., p. 221]. I think with Chrysostom, there is included also the idea of times whether seasonable or unseasonable to Timothy himself; not merely when convenient, but when inconvenient to thee, night as well as day (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>), in danger as well as in safety, in prison and when doomed to death as well as when at large, not only in church, but everywhere and on all occasions, whenever and wherever the Lord's work requires it.<div eID="gen37794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reprove--</hi>"convict," "confute."<div eID="gen37795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with, &c.--</hi>Greek, "IN (the element in which the exhortation ought to have place) all long-suffering (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, 25; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>) and teaching"; compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, "apt to teach." The Greek for "doctrine" here is didache, but in <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2Ti 3:16</reference>, didascalia. "Didascalia" is what one receives; "didache" is what is communicated [Tittmann]. <div eID="gen37796" type="x-p"/>

At my first answer--</hi>that is, "defense" in court, at my first public examination. Timothy knew nothing of this, it is plain, till Paul now informs him. But during his former imprisonment at Rome, Timothy was with him (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>). This must have been, therefore, a second imprisonment. He must have been set free before the persecution in A.D. 64, when the Christians were accused of causing the conflagration in Rome; for, had he been a prisoner then, he certainly would not have been spared. The tradition [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 2.251] that he was finally beheaded, accords with his not having been put to death in the persecution, A.D. 64, when burning to death was the mode by which the Christians were executed, but subsequently to it. His "first" trial in his second imprisonment seems to have been on the charge of complicity in the conflagration; his absence from Rome may have been the ground of his acquittal on that charge; his final condemnation was probably on the charge of introducing a new and unlawful religion into Rome.<div eID="gen37838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood with me--</hi>Greek, "came forward with me" [Alford] as a friend and advocate.<div eID="gen37839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may it not be laid to their charge--</hi>The position of "their," in the Greek, is emphatic. In order to depict his desertion, he informs Timothy that Erastus, one of his usual companions (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>, possibly the same Erastus as in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Ro 16:23</reference>, though how he could leave his official duties for missionary journeys is not clear), stayed behind at Corinth, his native place, or usual residence, of which city he was "chamberlain," or city steward and treasurer (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Ro 16:23</reference>); and Trophimus he left behind at Miletus sick. This verse is irreconcilable with the imprisonment from which he writes being the first: for he did not pass by Corinth or Miletus on his way to Rome when about to be imprisoned for the first time. As Miletus was near Ephesus, there is a presumption that Timothy was not at Ephesus when Paul wrote, or he would not need to inform Timothy of Trophimus lying sick in his immediate neighborhood.
